mechanisms: Perceived quality gaps in public schooling trigger migration to a limited functional sub-system, because parents evaluate schools by academic outcomes rather than proximity or default assignment.
Financial and informational scarcity converts zoning policy into a forced constraint, because affordability and local access override all other school attributes.
Higher parental education transforms school choice into an active marketplace search, because informed criteria like learner-teacher ratios and teacher passion become the filters for decision-making.
Perceived threats to safety and discipline turn schools into risk environments, because parental vigilance and willingness to exit become the primary safeguards for the child.
When traditional norms lose relevance, choice becomes preference-driven, because parents formulate new ideal-school aspirations and make trade-offs in pursuit of perceived quality.
evaluative_rules: Judge a school by perceived quality and academic outcomes, not by proximity or the default you were assigned.
When money and information are scarce, filter first on affordability and local access — every other attribute comes second.
If you have the means, search actively: visits, referrals and comparisons of teacher quality and class size beat accepting the default.
Weigh safety, supervision and discipline directly; a perceived risk to the child can veto everything else.
Where old norms no longer guide the choice, measure options against your own ideal of quality education and accept trade-offs to pursue it.
objection_patterns: Is this school in my zone, or will I be forced to accept it?
Can I afford the transport and fees, or is proximity my only real filter?
What do other parents say about discipline and safety here?
How do I find out about teacher quality and the curriculum before I enrol?
confidence: Multi-source qualitative synthesis drawing on author-interpretation and participant voice; single-province fieldwork with small samples — mechanisms are robust within the studied contexts, but magnitudes and national prevalence are unknown.
